findings.situation: Take a filer whose 2024 Schedule A, line 5d was $9,000: $2,000 of state income tax on line 5a plus $7,000 of real estate tax on line 5b. In 2025 the filer receives a $3,000 state income tax refund. The tool caps line 1 at the $9,000 total instead of the $2,000 of income taxes.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 90, Worksheet line 1: "But don’t enter more than the amount of your state and local income taxes shown on your 2024 Schedule A, line 5d"; question: "The amount on your 2024 Schedule A, line 5d (your state and local income or general sales taxes, real estate taxes and personal property taxes, added together)"
findings.why: Line 1 caps the refund at the income-tax part of line 5d, which is the line 5a amount, and only when income tax rather than sales tax was elected. The question gives the whole line 5d total, including real estate and personal property taxes, so the cap is too high. For a filer who elected sales tax, the cap should be zero ("None of your refund is taxable if ... you ... elected to deduct state and local general sales taxes", i1040gi p. 88), but the tool uses the line 5d total. These cases also fall under Exception 4 (i1040gi p. 89), which sends the filer to Pub. 525. No refusal for that exception is listed here, so the tool still applies the wrong cap.

findings.situation: A filer receives a Form 1099-G with box 8 checked, so the box 2 refund is of a tax that applies only to trade or business income, and the question tells them to include that box 2 amount in the total that feeds Schedule 1, line 1.
findings.source_text: f1099g p. 5: "Box 8. If this box is checked, the amount in box 2 is attributable to an income tax that applies exclusively to income from a trade or business ... If taxable, report the amount in box 2 on Schedule C or F (Form 1040), as appropriate." Question: "the total of box 2 of your Forms 1099-G (or a similar statement)"
findings.why: The box 8 amount belongs on Schedule C or F, not on Schedule 1, line 1. The question does not tell the filer to leave it out, so it flows through worksheet line 1 to s1.line1 and may also be reported on Schedule C or F.

findings.situation: A filer receives a state income tax refund in 2025 for tax year 2022 or 2023 (Form 1099-G box 3 shows a year other than 2024), and the question has them include it in the amount the worksheet tests against their 2024 Schedule A.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 88: "If the refund was for a tax you paid in 2024 and you deducted state and local income taxes on your 2024 Schedule A, use the State and Local Income Tax Refund Worksheet"; p. 89 Exception 1: "You received a refund in 2025 that is for a tax year other than 2024." Question: "State or local income tax refunds, credits or offsets you received in 2025"
findings.why: Worksheet line 1 is meant only for a refund of 2024 tax, limited by the 2024 Schedule A, line 5d. The question counts refunds for any tax year, and no listed refusal sends other-year refunds to Pub. 525.

findings.situation: A filer receives a refund from a jointly filed 2024 state return but is not filing a joint 2025 Form 1040 with the same person, and enters the full box 2 amount.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 89 Exception 9: "You received a refund because of a jointly filed state or local income tax return, but you aren’t filing a joint 2025 Form 1040 or 1040-SR with the same person"; p525 p. 24: "any refund ... must be allocated to the person that paid the expense"
findings.why: The worksheet needs only the filer's allocated share of the refund. The question asks for the whole box 2 total, and no listed refusal handles this case.
